strengths: Addresses a relevant NLP problem: predicting unsuccessful factual answers before generation. The frozen intermediate representations and small MLP provide a practical approach with low training and inference costs.

The experiments provide substantial evidence of predictive signal across four LLMs and three QA datasets, with additional HotpotQA results. FacLens is competitive with fine-tuning and generally improves over prompting, perplexity, and entity-focused alternatives. Table 2 reports 16 ms per prediction on LLaMA2-PQ.

Cross-model adaptation produces substantial improvements. For example, LLaMA2-to-Mistral transfer on EQ improves from 0.318 to 0.853 AUC, close to the target-supervised result of 0.854. Ablations examine question alignment, representation pooling, layers, and kernels.
The method is generally understandable, and the manuscript supplies a code link, model identifiers, dataset filtering rules, architecture details, and several optimization settings.
weaknesses: The central inference in Section 4.2 is invalid: comparable performance of pooled and individual probes does not establish equal conditional distributions P(y|X). A pooled MLP trained with labels from every domain can learn domain-specific functions when representations reveal model identity. Agreement between supervised predictions and t-SNE class separation do not resolve this issue. Linear-kernel MMD aligns feature means and provides no guarantee of class-conditional alignment. The claimed discovery of negligible concept shift therefore needs substantially stronger evidence or narrower wording.

The transfer experiments lack an important control for shared question difficulty. Because source and target training questions are identical, a target-representation probe trained directly with the existing source-model labels is a natural baseline requiring no target answer generation. A question-only predictor and evaluation on questions where source and target correctness disagree would further establish whether FacLens captures target-specific factuality. Current comparisons against unadapted probes do not isolate this contribution.

The claimed 97% label accuracy is insufficiently supported. Section 3.2 audits only 240 negative, string-matching examples while assuming all positive, non-matching examples are correctly labeled. Missing aliases and valid paraphrases can produce non-matches despite factual correctness. Both classes require auditing. The operational label also includes abstentions, so interpreting predictions as knowledge awareness or hallucination risk requires care.

Reproducibility of the label-free adaptation protocol remains incomplete. Appendix C.2 does not clearly specify DA stopping or checkpoint selection, while Figures 7 and 13 show target-test AUC over 1,000–1,400 epochs. The paper should identify which validation information selects checkpoints and kernels, and explicitly document shared question splits across models. These omissions leave uncertainty about reproducing transfer without target labels; they do not establish that leakage occurred.

No repeated-run variability or confidence intervals are reported, although several advantages over fine-tuning are small and the filtered NQ dataset contains only 1,244 questions. The assertion that sampling-based decoding preserves the conclusions lacks accompanying settings and results. The empirical findings are promising, but uncertainty in the central interpretation, label validation, and adaptation protocol prevents a clear Findings recommendation.
